{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Cauda equina syndrome (early or intermittent)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "L5 radiculopathy (e.g., from L4-L5 disc herniation or foraminal stenosis)", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic exertional compartment syndrome of the right calf", "confidence": 0.62}, {"diagnosis": "Peripheral arterial disease (intermittent claudication)", "confidence": 0.38}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.912, "reasoning": "The hallmark features—bilateral or unilateral leg symptoms worsening with upright posture and lumbar extension (e.g., treadmill incline), relieved by flexion/posterior pelvic tilt (e.g., sitting or bending forward), and reproducible with leg elevation above heart level—strongly point to neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis. The sole-of-foot tingling implicates S1 or L5/S1 nerve root involvement, while calf cramps suggest distal radicular or cauda equina irritation. The absence of vascular risk factors, lack of pallor/coldness, and complete resolution with rest (not just cessation of activity) make arterial claudication unlikely—classic PAD pain is not posture-dependent and does not improve *immediately* with rest; it typically requires >2 minutes and lacks the leg-elevation provocation. Cauda equina syndrome is less likely without bowel/bladder dysfunction or saddle anesthesia, but early or intermittent presentations can mimic stenosis. L5 radiculopathy fits the dermatomal (dorsum/lateral foot) and myotomal (dorsiflexion weakness, though not reported) pattern, but the exercise-triggered, posture-modulated nature favors central stenosis over isolated radiculopathy. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome is plausible given exertional calf cramps, but it would not explain the sole tingling or leg-elevation provocation, nor would it resolve *within seconds/minutes* of rest (typically takes 15–30 min)."}

The positional exacerbation (extension narrows the central canal and foramina) and symptom reproducibility with activity are classic. Cauda equina syndrome is less likely given absence of bowel/bladder dysfunction or saddle anesthesia, but early/intermittent presentations can mimic stenosis; hence moderate confidence. S1 radiculopathy is plausible given sole tingling and calf cramps, but isolated radicular pain typically lacks the exertional, posture-dependent, rapidly reversible pattern of claudication—though overlap exists with foraminal stenosis. Peripheral arterial disease is considered because of exertional calf cramps and relief with rest, but the positional trigger (worsening with leg elevation—not dependency) and prominent sensory symptoms (tingling sole) are atypical for ischemia; arterial claudication usually worsens with walking *and* improves with standing still *or* sitting, not specifically with leg lowering. Tarsal tunnel syndrome is unlikely: it causes localized medial ankle/sole paresthesias but is not posture- or exertion-dependent in this fashion, nor does it cause true calf cramping or resolve so predictably with brief rest."}
